Peak writing is when the villain stops sounding evil and starts sounding right.

Tobey Maguire’s Spider-Man is still one of the most relatable superhero portrayals ever put on screen.

Peter spends the trilogy dealing with loss, heartbreak, money problems, and the weight of being Spider-Man. He constantly has to choose between the life he wants and the responsibility he feels he can’t walk away from.

And then there’s Willem Dafoe’s Green Goblin, who gives Peter one of the most brutally honest warnings in the trilogy:

“One thing they love more than a hero is to see a hero fall.”

It perfectly captures the reality of being a hero. People will cheer for you when you save them, but the moment you fail, they can turn against you.

That idea hits even harder after Spider-Man: No Way Home. Peter loses Aunt May, MJ, Ned, and everyone who knows him. He’s completely alone, with no one even remembering who he is.

And yet, he keeps going.

He still puts on the mask.

Because that’s what makes Peter Parker a hero. Not the powers, the fame, or the suit.

It’s choosing to do the right thing, even when there’s nothing left for you to gain.
